title: Gateless Barrier, Case 12: Juiyen Calls Master
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The talk explores the idea of coming into maturity through embracing life's natural cycles, just like nature responds to changing seasons. This is illustrated through a Zen case about Suigan Calls Master, who remains true to his nature despite 30 years of practice and the influence of external thoughts and emotions. Ryushin Andrea Thach suggests that true mastery comes from taking responsibility for oneself and trusting one's inner guidance, rather than relying on external authority or codes of ethics.

sentences.text: Good morning, everyone.
Can you hear me all right?
Some of you are parked out in the North 40 out there, so if you can't hear me so well, please come a little closer.
What a beautiful day.

I was standing out waiting to come in for the last period of zazen, and I noticed that the maples that were planted out front are just about to bloom, and that their shadows are reflected in the window.
Everything is acting just as it should.
The trees are responding to the lengthening days and the warming air, and it's all taking its place as we are here.
The service we did this morning, did you feel it?
It was so still and open-hearted.
This enormous kindness was in the room.
I was very, very, very touched by what we're creating here.
What we're all creating, everyone taking their place so perfectly.
So this is day two of our sesshin to end practice period, and we've been studying what it means to take our place, or to come into and continue our process of maturation.
We've been studying different qualities in our shiso class, different qualities of maturing.
Qualities like patience and ethics and connection and responsibility.
That's one window in to cultivate in that way.
And I wonder what you all have seen as you've studied yourself in this process.
What you've reflected upon is your edge of maturation, where and how you're growing, the part of you that maybe doesn't want to grow up.
We get to see those aspects of ourselves so well in sesshin.
Zazen is our window in to who we really are: how we construct the world, how we lose our balance, avoid responsibility, want to cry out for mother or just chuck it sometimes.
Those are the growing edges, and at times we drop down and out of that.
As Nomon pointed to us yesterday, sometimes we're just at play, and that playing that we do is much like Ryokan's, the great poet's, playing with the children after he had obtained his enlightenment.
Picking daisies and weeds, dandelions, and putting them in his bowl, and forgetting to eat and forgetting to go begging.
That is a complete openness.
It seems paradoxical, but in that childlike way he is completely his full actualized self.

So if we're hanging by the limb of the tree with our teeth, we're wondering whether we should stay clamped on, or answer the great question of our life and take the risk to lose it all, or take the safe out and just stay stuck.
That's what we're studying here in sesshin.

I thought I would tag team with Nomon and talk about another case of the Mumonkan that has come up for me several times, and in conversation with different people in the sangha over the practice period.
It's one that I've heard a number of times in talks, and it has echoed in my own life.
It's called Suigan Calls Master, case 12.
The case goes something like this.
It's very simple.
*Every day Master Suigan calls out to himself, "Oh, master," and then he turns and he answers himself, "Yes."
"Are you awake?"
And then he would answer, "Yes, I am."
"Never be deceived by others any day, any time."
"No, I will not."*
*"Don't be deceived by anyone any day or any time."
"No, master, I will not."*
So, a little bit of background, and I actually think it's really interesting.
Suigan, whose Japanese name was Ryuyon, was born in the Tang dynasty, which is considered the Golden Age of Zen, and he was a student of the great Ganto.
Ganto was famous for his very pithy, direct statements, in the same vein as many other great teachers.
Gutei, in his one finger, his answer to everything was to point a finger, which he didn't understand until his master cut off one of his fingers, and then he really got what it was about.
Rinzai in his shout, and Eno in his original face.
So Ganto was a man of a direct way of expressing himself, and Suigan was also.
This was his one famous story, his one famous line, and you can pin everything on it.
I think it's also interesting to hear what his awakening story was with his teacher.
Sometimes someone that you respect will tell you something, and it will grab you because it doesn't make any sense, but there's something inside yourself that says, "But what is that?"
I've talked in here about what that story was for me with my first teacher, when I went crying to her and said, "I can't get my head around my sense of loneliness.
I can't get rid of it, and I can't live with it."
Her response to me was, "Don't ever think anything is out of place."
That phrase was a turning for me for a very long time, and has opened up.
And so I think that Suigan's awakening story is also very interesting.
He goes to his teacher, Ganto, and says, "What is the eternal truth?"
Don't we all want to know that, really seriously?
Come on, tell me what it is.
And the teacher says, "You've missed it."
"What do you mean I've missed it?
What did I miss?
Where is it?"
And his teacher says, "It is no longer the eternal truth."
Right.
Intuitively, we get that, but it sure took a really long time to chew that one over and digest it.
And so it has with me, with Suigan Calls Master, and so it has, I think, generally for people.
*Master, master, are you awake?
Yes, I am.
Don't be fooled by anyone any time.
No.*
That's usually understood as an ethical teaching, and it's not bad as an ethical teaching.
An ethical teaching is what we've somewhat been talking about, somewhat what arises when we sit zazen.
It's the first admonition in Dogen's Genjokoan: to study the self, to actually really come to see how the self arises in different situations.
Happy, relaxed, joyful self at times, lustful, craving self, under whatever conditions a certain being arises.
Don't be deceived by others, all the others that live inside of yourself.
Don't be deceived by your ideas of what you think is going on.
That's really sound advice, and it's worth a lifetime of study.
I think it's so much a lifetime of study that we fool ourselves to think that we ever get to the bottom of it.

Thirty years of practice later, sometimes under the right conditions, it's possible to still be just surprised at the place that's really fearful, the place that's really irritated, the place that's really desirous, that can come forward.
Whoa, where did that come from?
I thought I had dealt with that.
So it's important to always know that you can still be caught off guard.
So, "never to be deceived by others" is a tricky phrase.
It's not as simple as we think it can be.
Suigan early on is obviously a really capable student, and he thinks that he's starting to understand a little bit, and he has finished his study with his teacher, Ganto.
Maybe he wears a brown robe somewhere, I don't know.
He has an interview with another teacher, K-son, who asks him, "Where are you from?"
And he says, "Well, I'm from Lying Dragon Mountain."
That's L-Y-I-N-G, meaning it's the dragon's horizontal, not that he's telling fibs, which is where his teacher lived.
"I'm from Lying Dragon Mountain."
"Did the dragon rise up when you left there?"
Suigan, in answer, looks around him, like, "Yeah, he didn't come here."
K-son said, "You apply burning moxacure to skin which is already burned.
What's the use of you undergoing such torture?"
So Suigan's saying, "I think I got this one here," and K-son is saying, "I think you're fooling yourself."
K-son says nothing more to him, and Suigan digs himself in deeper.
He says, "Thusness is easy to deal with, not thusness is difficult to deal with.
If you are in a state of thusness, you are wide awake.
You are in neither thusness nor not thusness."
Total Zen nonsense.
But Suigan is feeling very proud of himself.
To which the teacher answers, "Today you have made a fool of me."
And Suigan must have felt very triumphant.
He walked out thinking that he had really aced this one.
It was not until many years later that he woke up and saw, "Oh my goodness, was it not I who was made a fool of?"
*Don't be fooled today, master.
No, I won't.*
What an admonition for him.
What an admonition for me, I don't know about you, to not be fooled by the way in which I think I see clearly sometimes, and I don't at all.
Or it really seems right, but maybe there's something I've missed.
This kind of begs the question of who the master is.
Usually we think the master is the person who knows everything, the guy who's in charge, the one who's got all the answers, someone who's been better or is in control of the situation.
But actually there is no grand plan, or anyone who is in charge.
So who's being fooled, and what does it mean to be fooled?
Can anyone actually fool us?
Can anyone actually pull the wool over the master's eyes?
When I was beginning to think about this koan, and really work it through about a month ago, I had a serendipitous story with one of my colleagues at work.
It just struck me as so apropos that I wanted to share it, and I wish I could say it with quite as much humor as she had.
My friend is a very capable nurse practitioner, and she's also the kind of person who's Johnny on the spot for anything that needs to be taken care of.

She's right there, she knows what to do, she's always spot on, she's [unclear: "uncharacteristically leading from the Pacific Northwest"], she's a very direct person, and she always seems to hit a bullseye.
So she and her husband are driving up in Canada during some of the snowstorms and icy roads, and they're driving along on the highway, and she sees this, is it a Ducati?
This really expensive kind of car, very high-end, $70,000, that is in front of them, that goes and then spins out and kind of rolls over.
Someone else pulls up, and they pull up, and the car is on its side, and the window rolls down, and the guy inside is throwing things out of the car, kind of like a crazy man.

Everyone else drives on, the other car drives on, but this guy's acting really bizarrely, and my friend gets out of the car and runs up to him and says, "We'll call the ambulance, stay calm, let's get you out of here, who knows what's going to happen to the car."
And he's still throwing stuff out of the car and acting crazy and refusing to go, saying, "No, I won't," and basically, "This shouldn't have happened, how is this going to get fixed?"
And he starts cursing out his mother.
His mother's to blame for him having rolled the car.
It's just totally crazy.
Well, the paramedics come, and apparently in Canada they can, she says, the paramedics talk to him, and he says, "I don't want to go anywhere."
But my friend, who's very medically astute, says, "He has to, there's something wrong with this guy."
They load him in their car and transport him to the nearest hospital.

He gets cleared there, but he's still kind of disoriented, I think, still wondering how this possibly could have happened to him, maybe he's still impugning his mother, This is a man who's in his 60s, who works for a big production company.
He's someone who's very successful by many standards.
He's a full grown-up, he's succeeded in many ways people aspire to, but here he's totally lost, and he has no way to get to the next town to have a place to stay at night.
So my friend and her husband take him, and he says to her, "Oh, you've been so," I missed a step.

My friend says, "You know, you've got to get your act together, you've got to grow up, there's something wrong with you, you've got to grow up," and this man looks at her and says, "Oh, you've been so helpful.
Can we have a cup of tea sometime?
Can I stay in touch?"
I don't know about you, but I think there's a little piece of some of us who have that inside of us: "Would someone just tell me how to grow up?
Would someone just tell me what I need to do in order to make my life right?
Right now, sometimes, would someone just figure it out?
I think I've done everything right."
Master, master, who is master?
Muman says in his poem, and that's what his teacher told him early on:
*Those who search the way do not realize the truth.
They only know their discriminating consciousness.
This is the cause of endless cycles of birth and death, yet ignorant people take it for the original man.*
That is the original face.
So what is this koan pointing at?
What is this mastery?
If it's not a code of ethics and no one is in charge, or if we say it's a code of ethics and someone's in charge, then there's always someone to blame and always someone to turn to.
But Uchiyama Roshi said that Zen is just about becoming an adult, just about growing up, that we take ultimate responsibility.
The maturity of Suigan that he's talking about is the maturity that you notice sometimes in people.
I think maybe you notice it in Norman Fischer.
I looked up his dharma name, Zoketsu, which means elephant grove.
Can you imagine anything more stable and stately than a bunch of elephants?
But you feel it in a person.
You understand that they're not going to be pulled off their feet, that whatever comes up, there's a kind of groundedness or stability.
"Don't be fooled, master" means don't go looking outside, you're settled inside.
As Suzuki Roshi says, you understand that you're completely supported from within.
I think about the experience of sesshin.
I was feeling this as we were getting ready to set up for the talk: there's such a sweet harmony in a well-functioning sesshin.

Have you noticed the servers arrive at a certain time, the pots are all there, they approach you and they bow and you bow, and somehow we eat food and the day moves along and we're ready to sit again, and everything just seems to find its place?
The Jisha puts the bowl right by your hand, and all of a sudden an offering is made and all the Buddhas and ancestors arrive.
Everything is functioning just as it needs to in order for sesshin, and we create it all.

That experience that we have of this kind of natural harmony of things unfolding is also the experience of living a ripe life, a mature life, and trusting in the unfolding of our life and circumstances moment after moment.
In his commentary, Shibayama, this set of commentaries I particularly like on the Mumonkan, calls this phenomenon of the master "absolute subjectivity."

It's an odd phrase actually, it's a little weird, but when you think about it, we usually think about the absolute as equating with what we call emptiness or nothing: nothing permanent, nothing existing inherently by itself.
Nothing in sesshin exists for any one sesshin element.
It really takes absolutely everything functioning together, and it functions together.
There are certain forms, there are certain things that we do, like codes of ethics, but golly, there are all kinds of things that come up in the course of a day that are unexpected.
Like the Doshi makes an extra pass to the altar when she's not supposed to, and the Doan times with it perfectly, puts down the striker and waits for the right moment.
There are all kinds of moments like that that happen.
So the subjectivity is that there's not a set idea of what is.
It's a response in the moment to what's happening, that arises out of what's going on.
Master, master, don't be fooled.
Right now, right here, what's happening?
Get your brain out of the way.
Get your ideas out of the way.
What's happening right now that you need to do?
That's the master's call.
Katagiri calls our practice being peace and harmony, right?
If you're in sync with what's needed and you flow with it, there's nothing that impedes what needs to happen.
It's very harmonious.
That's the quality that we have created here in this sesshin.
My old teacher calls monks being like milk and water.
Milk and water blend seamlessly.
You're unable to find the elements of milk or water in the mix.
They're perfectly harmonious with each other.
Thich Nhat Hanh, in his wonderful commentary on the Heart Sutra, says it's like sugar dissolved in a cup of tea.
Where are the molecules of sweetness?
You can't find them.
They're everywhere.
I think it's actually quite natural for us, even though it's a lot of hard work and endless years of Zen practice, to continually touch and act out of these places.
I actually think it's quite natural.
I recently heard a wonderful podcast.
I jumped places here.
We'll save that.
It'll still work.
I heard a wonderful podcast on creativity, and there was an interview with an astrophysicist named Margaret Geller.
Does anyone know Margaret Geller's work?
Phenomenal.
This woman somehow figured out how to map the universe.
Can you imagine standing in one little place on the earth and being able to map the entire universe?
That's crazy.
They went through the process of how it would be to be an alien looking down at earth and try to figure out how to map earth from one tiny view of it.
And what she found, maybe it doesn't matter so much, was that the galaxies cluster together.
They cluster in different ways, and there are vast places of black space.
And she said, you know, it is so beautiful.
She said our minds actually are really built to resonate with beauty, to gravitate to beauty, to turn towards it.
She said we're wired up to be in harmony.
Even the entire galaxy is wired up to be in harmony.
I find that very, very reassuring, to know that we are all wired up to be in harmony.
Can someone give me a time check?
I jumped around a little bit in what I was going to say.
Coming back to what it's like to practice in sesshin, we have certain forms, certain things we do, certain ways that we do them.
How do we harmonize with what it is that we're doing?
When we set cashews down in a bowl, do we drop them?
Do we lay them down, the cashews gently sliding into the bowl, aware of what we're doing?
In a way it's mindfulness, mindfulness with deep compassion, mindfulness with a complete sense of connection to the cashew and the ladle and the bowl that we're using.
When we play an instrument, we're not just making a sound where the striker is meeting the wood.
The wood is meeting the striker.
Our energy is to bring forth the sound of the striker and the sound of the drum or the sound of the bell.
And so there's a kind of relatedness that's not about a subject creating an object, but it's everything together making something happen in that moment.

And so to be aware of how we are and how we handle things and what we touch and how we relate with each other, to put our full being in, a sense of being completely a part of what's in front of us, the way we feel ourselves practicing as one organism.
Can we be complete with the zafu as we fluff it, complete in our bow to the server as we're receiving the food that we take?
Dogen has a couple of fascicles about this.
The longest fascicle in the Shobogenzo, his masterwork, is called Gyoji.
Gyoji means continuous practice.
Gyo means continuous practice.
Ji also means dignified, dignified practice.
Our dignified practice: I think that's what we see, that's what I see when I see someone like Norman or Shohaku Komura practice.
I see someone who's so completely in harmony with what they're doing, he's not using anything.
He's actually participating with it, fully in mastery of himself, and so there's no need to manipulate or to manhandle, to treat something roughly.
Dogen's other related fascicle is called Gyo-Butsu-ji, and that has different translations.
Okumura Roshi has translated it as "the dignified conduct of practice Buddha."
I've always loved that, practice Buddha.
Practice Buddha is your activity.
Whenever you're in action, whenever you're doing anything, you're practice Buddha.
You're manifesting practice, but you're the activity itself.
You and whatever else is going on with you is the activity itself.
The dignified is the same quality as the absolute subjectivity in the commentary, and the master, "Don't be fooled."
Don't let your mind manipulate you.
Show up completely to what you're doing here.
Get out of the way.
Finally, Katagiri Roshi calls this also "rules for being human."
This is the way we treat each other, the way in which we make our relations with neighbors, our partners, children, in our community, in our nation.
The rules for being human are about how we relate as if we're all one piece.
So there's a sequel to this koan, and that sequel, some hundreds of years later: I got the timing wrong, but here.
*One day a monk comes to see Master Gensha.
Gensha asks the newcomer, "Where have you been recently?"
"With Master Zwiegen, sir," replied the monk.
"I see.
In what manner does Master Zwiegen instruct his disciples?"
The monk reported in detail how Zwiegen would every day call out, "Oh master," and would answer himself.
Listening to the monk, Gensha asked again, "Why didn't you stay longer with Zwiegen to continue your training?"*
He actually didn't get it, did you?
*And the monk said, "Master Zwiegen died."
At this reply, Gensha asked the monk an unexpected question.
"If you call out to him now, 'Oh master,' will he answer?"*
Will he?
If you call out to him right now, will he answer you?
Right now, in this very moment, where is the master?
The teacher gives a response:
*Mountains respond to the temple bell in the moonlight.*
So let's listen and play on.
Thank you very much.
